prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

World like a coat, silver clasps, ermine lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket amongst the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening, world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider, world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing, I cannot hold you at all, it seems, your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much much, and I a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.

Here are three ways to polish the text, depending on the exact tone you wish to achieve. Because this is a deeply lyrical and evocative piece of writing, "professional" in this context means **refined, literary, and rhythmically precise** without losing its poetic soul.

### Option 1: Refined & Elegant Prose (Recommended)
*This version cleans up the syntax and rhythm while retaining the intimate, poetic voice and all original imagery.*

> The world was like a coat—fastened with silver clasps, lined in ermine, warm with the dead rolling within its crimson core. I believed then that everything had a purpose; this was back when I still drank. Wasn’t I a favored traveler, nestled in that pocket alongside butterscotch candies and matchbooks? Inessential, perhaps, yet accounted for—a steady anchor to touch. 
> 
> A world like a morning glory, wilting every evening; a world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder. I can hardly fathom how deeply I believed, or how that conviction took physical shape around my body—molding to my heat, acquiring substance. Whenever I was questioned, I offered it up, letting them touch the sleeve; I needed nothing. 
> 
> A world like an egret, poised and pale upon the highway median; a world like a regret typed out and promptly erased. I cannot draw you any closer without exposing us to the gaze of others; indeed, it seems I cannot hold you at all—neither your evergreens nor your curling potato vines. It is all simply overwhelming, and I am merely a speck of goose down, a wisp of thistle fluff—naked, hatless, unaccounted for, and extra. A world like a world like a world.

outputs.L2:
Here is a complete rewrite of the passage, retaining all of its original details, images, and meaning while using fresh phrasing and sentence structures:

I used to view the universe as a heavy jacket, fastened with metallic hooks and lined with plush fur, retaining the warmth of departed souls at its crimson core. During the era when alcohol was still part of my life, I was convinced that every single thing served a grand design. I felt like an extraordinary passenger, safely stowed in a coat pocket alongside hard sweets and boxes of matches—unimportant, perhaps, yet recognized and providing a steady, reassuring presence to lean on. 

To me, reality was like a blossom that wilts every evening, or a frightened hound cowering at the sound of thunder. Looking back, my depth of faith astonishes me—how that conviction cast a physical mold around my frame, absorbing my body's heat until it turned solid. Whenever doubters questioned my view, I proudly offered the garment for them to touch its sleeve; I was entirely self-sufficient. 

The universe seemed like a motionless white heron perched on a highway median, or a message of regret keyed into a screen only to be deleted. Now, I find I cannot pull this existence any closer without drawing everyone's attention—in truth, I am completely unable to grasp it at all, with its dense pines and creeping vines. Its grandeur utterly overwhelms me. By comparison, I am merely a drifting bird feather, a speck of weed seed, exposed and bare-headed, overlooked and redundant, while the earth simply remains an endlessly repeating reality, world after world after world.
outputs.L3:
There was a time when I moved through life under the quiet assurance of an overarching purpose. I believed, with a devotion so deep it required no proof, that the universe was governed by a grand design—and that I occupied a secure, deliberate place within its vast architecture. This conviction was not a mere abstract thought; it felt remarkably physical. It was a tangible weight of comfort, a heavy, protective mantle that shielded me from the cold winds of existential doubt and the gnawing ache of unfulfilled desire. Wrapped in that certainty, I felt anchored and invulnerable to the chaos lurking at the edges of consciousness.

Over time, however, the metaphors by which I understood existence began to fracture and shift. The fortress of my early beliefs dissolved into something far more fluid and precarious. I started to see the world not as an enduring monument, but as a delicate ecosystem defined by impermanence—a landscape marked by shifting light, fleeting moments of breathtaking beauty, and the quiet, persistent residue of regret. Reality revealed itself to be profoundly vulnerable, a sequence of brief, luminous flashes caught between what has passed and what will inevitably fade.

With this revelation came a dizzying change in scale. The world suddenly expanded into an overwhelming immensity, its staggering vastness impossible to comprehend, let alone contain. Where I once felt a sense of intimacy and belonging, I now experience an inescapable vertigo. The immense weight of existence has become too large to grasp; its moments slip through my fingers like water, leaving nothing for me to hold onto. 

Stripped of my former certainty, I stand in the open, fragile and entirely exposed. The comforting shield of grand purpose has vanished, leaving me to navigate a universe that operates without regard for my presence. I am no longer the protected center of a coherent story. In the quiet expanse of this boundless, indifferent world, I am finally left with a stark and haunting truth: I am unmoored, vulnerable, and ultimately unaccounted for.
outputs.L4:
There was a time when the world fit me like a heavy wool coat, tailored precisely to the contours of my shoulders. Its lining was soft with intention, woven from the comforting conviction that every event—the sudden rainfall, the falling leaf, the quiet turning of the seasons—was orchestrated for my benefit, or at least my understanding. In those years, the universe felt intimate and small enough to wrap around myself against the chill of uncertainty. 

I walked through life draped in these transient shelters of my own making. The sky was a painted ceiling built to protect me; the morning wind was a breath meant to cool my face. Even when misfortune struck, I wore it like a rough-spun scarf, believing it was not random chance, but a carefully measured lesson designed to strengthen the fabric of my character. I lived inside a grand, self-centered myth: the belief that existence was fundamentally *for* me—a warm room in which I was the central, cherished occupant.

Yet, time is a quiet thread-puller. Slowly, imperceptibly at first, the seams began to yield. The heavy wool grew thin, worn down by the sheer, unyielding weight of reality. 

I began to notice that the rain did not fall to invite my contemplation; it fell because atmospheric pressure demanded it, soaking the earth with complete indifference to who stood beneath it. The sun did not rise to illuminate my path; it burned out of violent hydrogen combustion, utterly unconcerned with whether I opened my eyes to witness its light. The events I had once interpreted as personal omens or tailored trials were revealed to be nothing more than the cold, mechanical turning of an unguided wheel.

Piece by piece, the protective garment dissolved. The warm coat disintegrated into loose threads, then into dust, carried off by a wind that blew only because the air was cold in one place and warm in another. The comforting illusion that every tragedy contained a hidden, benevolent purpose evaporated, leaving behind only the stark, unvarnished geometry of the cosmos. The world was no longer a hearth built to keep me warm; it was an ocean, vast and fathomless, entirely untamed by human meaning.

Now, I stand fully exposed. The cold air of an indifferent universe rushes against my skin, unfiltered by the soft lies I once wore. There is a profound, terrifying vulnerability in this nakedness. Without the armor of divine personal attention, every shadow feels darker, every silence deeper, and the sheer scale of the world threatens to crush my fragile sense of self. I am no longer the hero of a cozy, contained narrative; I am a fleeting spark suspended in an infinitely sprawling void.

Yet, alongside the terror of this detachment, a quiet, undeniable clarity remains. The world has not grown hostile; it has simply revealed its true nature, unbounded by my desperate need for comfort. Stripped of my warm coat and standing unprotected in the wind, I feel the full weight of my smallness—fragile, detached, and utterly alone, yet finally seeing the vast, unstitched wild of reality as it truly is.
outputs.L5:
In a **world** obsessed with addition—more noise, more speed, and endless collection—we often lose sight of the quiet beauty found in subtraction. From an early age, we are taught to hoard, mistaking the **unessential** for the vital. We gather trivial worries, digital clutter, and superficial ambitions, convincing ourselves that every minor urgency demands our soul's full weight. 

But **when** do we finally stop to breathe? 

There comes a crucial turning point, a moment **when** the illusion shatters and clarity takes its place. It might happen during a late-night walk under a silent sky, or in the sudden stillness after a heavy rain. In that pause, the frantic rhythms of the modern **world** fall away, revealing just how much of what we carried was entirely **unessential**. 

**When** we strip away the noise of what doesn't truly matter, we discover what actually does: the warmth of genuine connection, the peace of the present moment, and the simple truth that we were complete all along.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic prose poem using a series of repeating similes ("World like a...") that explores themes of lost faith, sobriety, and feeling small or insignificant against the weight of the universe.
counterfactuals.output:
The ice has melted into lukewarm water, and the sharp, clinical light of morning finds every crack in the plaster. World like a scrubbed floor, pale and sterile, stripped of the sweet, amber blur that used to soften its edges. I sit with my palms flat on the wood, entirely sober, feeling the terrifying, unvarnished weight of my own pulse. World like an empty tabernacle, its incense burned down to grey ash, its holy doors left swinging in the draft. I used to pray until my throat was raw, believing the silence was merely a divine pause, but now I understand the heavens are only cold air, cosmic dust, and quiet arithmetic. 

World like a drained glass, dry at the bottom, offering no communion and no relief. Without the poison to make the small room feel infinite, the room is just a box, and I am just the fragile thing trapped inside it. World like a moth beating against the glass of an abandoned lighthouse, striving toward a flame that went out centuries ago. I look up through the window at the night sky, at the ancient light of dead stars bleeding across the black, and the scale of it crushes the breath from my chest. We were taught that we were made in an image, but the universe does not know my name; it does not even know the shape of my guilt. 

World like a grain of salt dissolved in a dark, bottomless sea, so impossibly tiny it leaves no trace, no taste, no memory. There is no god in the glass, no angel in the ceiling, only the quiet tick of the kitchen clock measuring a life that has finally run out of excuses to hide. World like a stone dropped down a dry well, falling through the vast, dark quiet, waiting for a splash that will never come.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of lyrical prose about outgrowing a safe, comforting illusion, incorporating sensory details like coat pockets, butterscotch, morning glories, and thistles.
counterfactuals.output:
For years, the universe was small enough to be tucked away, folded neatly into the dark, wool-lined depths of my coat pockets. Inside that sheltered haven, my fingers would absentmindedly trace the smooth, cellophane-wrapped squares of butterscotch, their golden sweetness a promise that the world would always be mild, predictable, and warm. 

I lived beneath a ceiling of spun sugar and soft assumptions. Around the porch lattice, the morning glories unfurled their fragile indigo trumpets each dawn, painted in colors so vivid they convinced me daylight would never bruise. It was easy to rest inside that sanctuary of silk and sugar, to believe that love was a thing that only built walls, never broke them, and that safety was the highest form of truth. 

But warmth, when kept too long in a sealed room, turns stale. The butterscotch grew cloying, a heavy syrup lingering at the back of my throat, a reminder of a comfort I had outgrown but was too afraid to spit out. The morning glories, paper-thin and delicate, began to feel less like a welcome and more like a curtain, hung carefully to hide the vast, unscripted horizon beyond the gate. 

One morning, the air shifted. The sleeves of the coat felt tight across my shoulders; the old hideaway had shrunk around me. I pulled my hands out of those deep pockets, leaving the crinkled wrappers and the lint-dusted candies behind in the dark. 

I walked past the lattice, stepping off the manicured lawn and onto the raw, unpaved ridge beyond. There, the earth did not soothe; it demanded. The wild pasture was thick with thistles, standing proud and defiant, their purple crowns bristling with silvery, sharp spines. When I brushed against them, they tore at my hemlines and pricked my bare wrists. 

The sting was sharp, sudden, and entirely unadulterated. It was not the soft, padded kiss of the illusion, but the fierce, cold bite of the actual. Standing there, bleeding just enough to feel the cold wind clear my lungs, I realized the lie had kept me warm, but only the thistles could make me awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a surreal, emotional prose poem in the style of Richard Siken about grief, intimacy, and the overwhelming nature of existence.
counterfactuals.output:
Put your hand inside my mouth and tell me if it’s still raining outside. We are sitting on the linoleum of a room that keeps expanding, the walls backing away from us like timid animals, and I am trying to remember which one of us is dead. You have blood on your knuckles and I have the sun stuck in my throat, hot and heavy and impossible to swallow. Tell me again about the rescue squad. Tell me how we get out of a body when the doors are welded shut. 

I wanted to paint a target on your chest just so I’d know where to press my face when the sky starts coming down. Listen to me: the world is too loud, it is bursting through the windowpanes like a stray dog, it is biting at our ankles. I loved you so hard my ribs cracked into kindling and now everything is on fire. Your shadow is stuck to the wallpaper. I try to peel it off with a fingernail, but it just bleeds onto my shoes. 

*Breathe,* you say, but the air is thick as wet plaster. You reach into my shirt to pull out the hurt, but your fingers just come back dripping with light. Is this what we bargained for? All these miles of empty highway inside the ribcage, all this noise. We are two bad accidents trying to apologize to the wreckage. Look at your hands. Look at mine. We tore open the afternoon to see what was making that terrible humming sound, and now we can't get the darkness back into the box. 

Don't look at the door. There’s nothing out there but more space, miles and miles of black velvet and cold teeth. Lie down on the floor with me. Put your mouth on my collarbone until the engine stops turning. I am holding on to you so tightly that we are turning into the same person, a double-headed monster in a burning hallway, screaming at the paramedics to just leave us alone, just let us finish burning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short monologue from the perspective of a recovering alcoholic reflecting on how their old beliefs used to shield them, ending with a breakdown of language.
counterfactuals.output:
I built an entire cathedral out of *'I'm just a sensitive soul.'* That was the magic of it. The drinking wasn't just a habit; it was a doctrine. I told myself I was an artist drowning out the static, or a hard worker taking the edge off a cruel world. What a beautiful, bulletproof armor that was. As long as I was a tragic hero, I didn’t have to admit I was just a coward hiding in a bottle. The booze gave me a grand dialect—a way to turn my own destruction into poetry. It kept the cold out. It kept the truth away.

But you take away the glass, and the story collapses. The armor melts into sludge. 

Now I’m standing out in the raw weather, exposed to everything. No grand narrative. No tragic poetry. Just... this. Just the scraping sound of reality. 

I try to explain how it feels, to put a name on this... this vast, bright, terrifying room I'm suddenly stuck in, but the... the grammar won't hold. The words, they... they used to shield me, but now they just crumble. 

I want to say *I am healing*, but *healing* is... what is... h-h-healing? It’s just a sound. A shape my mouth makes. 

The stories are gone. The logic is... it's thin. Paper thin.

I am... I... 

The clock is... tick. T-t-tick. 

It’s too quiet. Or too loud. I can't... the sentences aren't... 

I am just... breath. Out. In. 

B-breath. 

No words left for it. Just... air. 

Just...

...here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose poem that begins with the image "World like a coat" and ends with the phrase "the world like a world like a world."
counterfactuals.output: World like a coat, heavy-wooled and stained at the cuffs with salt and diesel, buttoned tight against a wind that smells of iron and wet cedar. I slip my hands into its deep, dark pockets and find the detritus of lost seasons: a smooth river stone still holding yesterday’s sun, a scrap of paper with an address that no longer exists, the soft gray lint of forgotten afternoons. It sags at my shoulders, trailing its frayed hem through the slush of dawn, too large for a single heart yet impossible to take off. I pull the collar up around my ears to drown out the low hum of the stars. When a thread snags on a thorn, a whole town unravels into gray yarn; I must stop by the roadside to stitch the horizon back into the lining. But under this heavy weave, the body warms itself. It learns the weight of gravity as a kindness, the stiff wool softening where the elbows bend. And one day, the last button will give way, slipping silently into the deep grass, and the garment will fall open to reveal no skin at all, only light turning into light, breathing into the vast, unstitched sky, leaving behind the fabric to step entirely inside the world like a world like a world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
